To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

5'-flanking region of gene A is organized as a complex with at least 5 DNase I-hypsensitive sites; these sites are present on liver chromatin but absent on kidney chromatin; they correspond to the L promoter and to 2 novel control sequences; the L promoter is active in liver but silent in kidney; this is due to the presence of a methylation-sensitive control element in the promoter region.
DNase I-hyposensitive sites are present on liver chromatin but are not detectable in kidney, and that the L promoter is demethylated in the adult but methylated during development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of regulatory sequences on the gene for 6-phospho- fructo-2 kinase/fructose-2-6 bisphosphatase.
the identification on gene A in situ of sequences involved in its tissue-specific expression.
the identification of regulatory regions on gene A and with the characterization of the mechanisms involved in the control of the tissue specificity of its L promoter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNase I-hyper-sensitive sites are a reflection of the activity of a gene and that DNA methylation pattern is a reflection of the developmental status of the gene.

the L-promoter activity in liver is due to the combined action of a number of cis-acting regulatory elements, which include a glucocorticosteroid-responsive unit and a number of DNase I-hyper sensitive sites, some of which are located within a region of demethylated DNA.
sites L1, L2, and I2 are cis-acting elements for the L-type transcription, and that the DNA methylation pattern around the L promoter is a prerequisite for its activity in liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gene A is regulated in a tissue-specific manner by a combination of cis-acting sequences and DNA methylation.
the L promoter is activated by demethylation of the 5' region of gene A and by DNase I-hypermethylation of the L promoter itself.
the L promoter is activated in liver by a combination of tissue-specific DNase I hypersensitivity and demethylation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNase I-hypermethylation and demethylation of the 3'-untranslated region of the L promoter may be important for the tissue- and developmental stage-specific regulation of gene A.
DNase I-hypermethylation assays can be used to identify cis-acting sequences on a large scale, even when the transcriptional activity of the gene is not known.
the L promoter is not a simple transcriptional unit but a composite of elements whose combination is required for its activity in liver.
